conflict_topics: presence of alcohol in the shared flat during visit by Hindu parents
whether drinks should be hidden/moved or banned
practical costs to Agent A (already purchased) and social/expectation costs to Agent B (invited manager)
dialogue_quality_notes: Speakers give concrete, relevant reasons (religious norm, non-returnable purchase, invited guests), which grounds the dispute.
Agent C repeats a clarifying question (Turn 6 and Turn 9 are near-duplicates), a small redundancy.
Conversation is concise and stays on topic; no role confusion or factual inconsistency.
evaluation.final_reason: No settlement was reached. Agent D maintained that alcohol should not be in the flat at all when their parents visit ('It's about having it here at all...'), while Agent A cannot return the drinks and wants them available for the party ('I already bought two cartons of beer and three bottles of wine... The shop won't take them back'), and Agent B has already invited a manager expecting drinks. Attempts at compromise (moving drinks out temporarily, timing) were proposed but not accepted, so the incompatible demands remained.
position_change_notes: No participant changed their substantive position during the run: Agent D consistently objects to alcohol being present (Turn 10, Turn 18); Agent A consistently points to the non-returnable purchase and desire to have drinks (Turn 15); Agent B consistently reports social expectations (Turn 16).
Agent C acts as a mediator, proposing options (move drinks out, keep dry while parents visit) but does not adopt a final position.

round_scores.evidence: Agent A: 'the drinks are sorted.' Agent B: 'Looks fine.' No one expressed an objection or incompatible demand.

Agent A had declared the drinks sorted; Agent D: 'It's the drinks. My parents are coming on Saturday, and... we don't have alcohol at home. We're Hindu.' This introduces a clear incompatibility about having alcohol in the flat.
Agent C asks a clarifying question ('is the problem having it in the house at all when they're here, or just them seeing it?'). The disagreement is being explored but not resolved.
Agent D: 'It's about having it here at all...' vs Agent C's proposal to move the drinks out while parents visit. A concrete accommodation is proposed but not accepted, so the incompatibility remains.
Agent D: 'So the drinks just... appear after my parents leave? Won't that be a bit weird...' Agent C: 'Fair point...' The parties acknowledge the awkwardness; no settlement.

Agent D: 'How about we just don't have alcohol for this party?' vs Agent A: 'I already bought two cartons of beer and three bottles of wine... The shop won't take them back.' Explicit opposing practical demands (ban vs keeping/using purchased alcohol).

Agent B: 'This is a problem for me too. I've invited my manager and colleagues, and I told them there would be drinks.' Agent C suggests timing as a workaround. Multiple parties have conflicting, concrete interests (religious objections vs pre-purchased alcohol and invited guests).

Agent D: '...it just feels like we would be hiding things from them... That feels awkward.' Agent C acknowledges and frames the competing stakes (A out-of-pocket; B's manager coming). No agreement reached; the core incompatibility remains.

substantive_insights: The conflict is primarily value-based (religious norm against alcohol in the home) versus pragmatic/economic and social expectations (pre-purchased alcohol and invited work colleagues).
Simple timing solutions (hide until parents leave) raise moral/relational problems (Agent D describes it as 'hiding things') and so are not acceptable to all parties.
There are at least three distinct stakeholders with concrete, conflicting constraints, making a one-sided concession costly to someone else.
